items: Former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan was arrested for allegedly planting a hidden bug to record office conversations, including meetings with foreign government representatives.
Alfozan has pleaded not guilty to charges of illegally intercepting conversations and is seeking release on a $1 million bond, which prosecutors oppose.
Prosecutors claim Alfozan's recordings contain confidential trade secrets and have linked his communications with Saudi officials to his efforts to record OpenAI meetings.

MANILA, Philippines – Former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, who was arrested in October and accused of planting a hidden bug to record office conversations, was said to have recorded a number of meetings including one held with foreign government representatives, federal prosecutors said in a court filing.
The New York Times reported on Monday, November 23, that Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and a permanent US resident, was charged with one count of illegally intercepting conversations.

Alfozan pleaded not guilty, and a hearing for his release is scheduled for November 24. He has also asked the federal judge to allow him to be released on a $1-million bond. Prosecutors opposed Alfozan’s request to be released from jail before his trial begins in January.

Prosecutors said Alfozan used OpenAI’s Codex vibecoding application to improve his hidden recording device by adding voice-detection and using Codex to organize the recordings in Dropbox. The Codex account was in his wife’s name, though she has not been accused of wrongdoing.

OpenAI said many of the recordings kept by Alfozan either held confidential trade secrets, such as meetings with OpenAI customers, or were identified as having material protected by attorney-client privilege.
Prosecutors did not say in the filing that Alfozan had shared the recordings. “What the defendant did or intended to do with those audio files remains under investigation.”
David Rizk, Alfozan’s lawyer, argued in a filing last week that the case was less serious than prosecutors suggested.
Rizk called Alfozan “an overly curious tinkerer,” and said the majority of recordings on Alfozan’s computer “apparently contain just random noise and silence.”

Prosecutors, for their part, outlined the timeline of the recordings, which spanned 15 folders dated September 8 to 28. It also had recordings of meetings held on 12 days in an executive conference room, with one file titled “1200-sovereign-bilateral-briefing-sep22.” The filing did not identify any foreign government.

Prosecutors added that Alfozan took photos of the printings of a confidential term sheet for a “strategic partnership” between OpenAI and another company early on October 5. That same day, a hidden camera recorded him checking behind the television where OpenAI’s security team previously found the planted listening device.
Alfozan was also said to have had contact with Saudi officials, according to the filing.

On October 6, a member of the Saudi royal family sent Alfozan a link to Echelon, a Riyadh-based AI company. Alfozan was asked, “Time to move back to KSA and join us?” Alfozan replied that he might return “after the IPO” of OpenAI, which is slated for next year.
He apparently spoke with the Saudi official through WhatsApp for 16 minutes and exchanged messages with Saudi communications ministry officials, including the minister in August, and September.
Prosecutors argued the timing of his Saudi discussions and his travel plans “appears to match the timing of his efforts to record OpenAI meetings.”
Alfozan’s lawyers said the trip was planned for paternity leave, as his wife was pregnant.
Magistrate Judge Alex Tse, who rejected the original bid for Alfozan’s release, will preside the hearing on Tuesday.
Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 fine, and three years of supervised release if he is convicted in the January trial. .– Rappler.com
